title: Setting Up Cypress E2E Tests for an Enterprise Laravel App
summary: How I approached end-to-end testing for an internal enterprise web app during an internship: choosing what to automate, structuring specs, and pairing them with Swagger-documented APIs.
points: The team manually re-tested critical user flows every release cycle. Regression testing took days, and recurring issues still slipped through.
We prioritized automation by risk: authentication, core user workflows, and data submission flows first. Edge-case UI states stayed manual.
Cypress specs were grouped by user flow, not by page. Each spec read like the scenario a QA would write down: setup, action, assertion, teardown.

Because the REST APIs were documented in Swagger, API-level checks could be cross-referenced with the UI steps they backed - when a UI test failed, we could tell whether the defect lived in the frontend or the backend contract.
The scripts became the regression baseline: manual QA cycles shrank to exploring new features, while the critical paths were guarded on every run.

title: Catching Data Inconsistencies in a Go + MySQL Backend
summary: Patterns I used while building backend services for a workforce management app: SQL-driven validation to catch inconsistencies before they spread into reports.
points: A workforce management app is only as trustworthy as its data. Roster mismatches and duplicated records surfaced as wrong reports downstream.

Validation lived at multiple layers: struct-level checks in Go handlers using the Gin framework, database constraints in MySQL, and SQL queries used as diagnostic tools to audit incoming data batches.

For Excel and PDF imports, we validated before committing: staging the data, running SQL consistency checks for nulls, duplicates, and referential integrity, and only then writing into the live tables.
Troubleshooting followed the same path - when reports looked off, SQL queries against the affected tables usually located the inconsistency faster than tracing application logs.
The lesson: in data-heavy backends, SQL is not just a persistence layer - it is a debugging and validation instrument.

title: Designing a Modular Laravel–Flask Backend for IoT Air Quality Forecasting
summary: Architecture notes from my thesis: why we split a Laravel backend and a Flask ML microservice into a 4-layer design, and what load testing revealed.
points: The problem: air quality monitoring needs continuous ingestion from distributed IoT sensors plus forecasting - two workloads with very different rhythms.
We separated concerns into four layers: Device (sensors), Service (API and ingestion), Data (PostgreSQL), and Presentation (dashboard with role-based access).
Laravel handled relational data management and the API surface. The Prophet forecasting model ran as an independent Flask microservice - so model retraining never blocked ingestion.

Performance testing measured an average API response time of 557 ms and throughput of 1.34 requests per second. Stress testing exposed a 24.18% error rate under heavy load - a clear signal for where optimization was needed.
The evaluation was published as a peer-reviewed paper at IEEE ICoDSA 2025, and the numbers above come directly from that paper.

title: Shipping a Full-Stack Rental App Solo in 5 Days: Campkit
summary: 26 commits in 5 days: how I sequenced a camping-gear rental platform - backend and migrations first, then auth, then admin and user frontends, then bugfix.
points: The scope: a rental platform where customers browse gear, book it, and track borrowing history - while admins manage products, confirm returns, and organize categories.
Day 1-2 went to the foundation: project structure, database migrations with Sequelize, and the backend endpoints. Nothing renders without data, so data came first.
Day 3 was auth: login and register pages for both user and admin shells, wired to the API before any feature screens existed.
Day 4 split into the two frontends: the user flow (browse, book, history, profile) and the admin console (products, returns, categories). Building them against the same API kept both consistent.
Day 5 was bugfix and README. The commit history tells the story honestly - including the fixes - which is exactly what a reviewer wants to see in a solo sprint.
